newsitem.title: INDIA: FEATURE - Indian consumers take to credit cards.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Indian consumers take to credit cards.

text.p: Indian wallets are getting heavier these days, and it's not just due to cash.
Plastic money has firmed its grip as the traditionally credit-averse Indian consumer has taken quickly to the buy-now-pay-later idea.
India's credit card market is growing at an annual rate of more than 35 percent, market analysts say.
In urban India, middle class citizens no longer love ideals of thrift championed by the nation's founding father, Mahatma Gandhi. The credit card is a status symbol to be flaunted.
A national income growth of more than six percent in recent years has put more spending power into the country, and consumer finance and credit cards are seen as a logical extension.
"The credit card is going to emerge as the best form of consumer lending with regard to growth rate and profitability," Pushpendra Mehta, a credit card consultant, told Reuters.
India has an estimated two million credit card users at present and the industry expects the figure to reach 15 million by 2001, Mehta said.
MIDDLE CLASS OFFERS POTENTIAL
"The credit card market is emerging as the centre-piece of banking relationships. It is an attractive proposition to get into, with a very high rate of growth," Mehta said.
The scope is enormous.
Members of India's middle class, estimated at anywhere between 200 and 400 million, are all potential card holders, making India one of the world's big potential markets, Mehta said.

"Not everyone wants a holiday in the Caribbean. Mastercard is concentrating on things like buying a train ticket or petrol and that culture is creeping in," said Ajay Bhalla, marketing director of Mastercard in India.

Mastercard is the current leader with about 60 percent of the market share, and had 1.3 million credit card users in India last year. Visa, which has between 30 and 35 percent, completes a virtual carving up of the market between the two labels.
Retail banking, consumer finance and plastic money took off in India after 1991, when the country launched a sweeping economic liberalisation programme.
The ground was laid shortly before that.
ANZ Grindlays says it was the first to start selling plastic money in India, in 1989, with its Visa card.
A NEW STATUS SYMBOL
Diner's Club was already there, but being a charge card, it was not seen as the true harbinger of the credit card culture.
For many, plastic money is a status symbol. For others it is a safety device against pickpockets and sudden overspending.
"It gives me easy payment options, and is convenient to use," said Paraj Kakkar, a business executive and a frequent traveller.
"It helps me in my times of adversity. Who else will lend me money today if I am outside the city?," financial consultant Sanjeev Ailawadi said.
With nearly 40 percent of India's 930 million people not assured of basics such as food, clothing and shelter, credit cards are out of reach for all but the affluent.
India's per capita income is around $70 a year, and credit card firms usually seek proof of earnings of at least $150 a month.
But in absolute numbers, the top crust of India is enough to make for a juicy market.
"The number of millionaires in India might be equal to the population of a small European country," said Badal Mukhopadhyay, economist at the Delhi School of Economics.
FOREIGN BANKS LEAD THE WAY
While India's mammoth state-owned banks have floated credit card businesses, they do not have their own grip on the business, and are currently affiliated to Visa or Mastercard.
Foreign banks have a 65 percent share of the credit card market, thanks to aggressive marketing, Mehta said.
"Foreign banks have looked at it as an independent profit centre while Indian banks are awakening to the potential of this market only now," he said.
The biggest challenge for credit card firms is the small-town shopkeeper, who increasingly accounts for big sales but still prefers old-fashioned cash to fancy plastic.
Bigger stores enjoy any free publicity that credit card companies may give them, but neighbourbood establishments in most Indian cities do not yet accept plastic.
"My local drug store does not accept a credit card and neither do most of the petrol stations," says Manmohan Bhutani, a corporate executive just back from working abroad.
"The time they take to process the transaction is very high compared to other countries," he added.

"India is very much part of the Asian ethos where people don't like to incur credit," said Anita Gupta, head of corporate affairs at Citibank which franchises more than 50 percent of the credit cards in the country.
"Secondly it (card money) leaves an audit trail," Gupta added, referring to inspection by tax authorities, which millions of India's newly-rich want to avoid.
Barely 14 million out of India's population of 950 million are taxpayers.
Assessing potential customers also poses problems for the credit card companies.
"There are no credit bureaux to rate the creditworthiness of a person, and that also hampers the growth of the business," Gupta said.
